doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Newtown High, the Grossos, Condon's and his school jazz band
summary: At Newtown High he met Bobby Grosso and his father Joe, visited Eddie Condon's, and led a school Dixieland band with Larry O'Brien.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: You know so I was 14, that would have been 19 — what is it 35, 45 — 1949. I was just about to go into high school.
And you’d been playing clarinet for a few years.

About four years, three or four years. I don’t remember how serious it was, but I remember playing, you know with the piano playing the “Twelve Street Rag” at an assembly period. “Now we’ll see ‘The Heavens are Telling’ by Ludwig von Beethoven to be followed by John Kenneth Davern performing on the clarinet “The Twelfth Street Rag.” And I remember how awful it was trying to finger the Albert System playing because [scats] I got messed up. So yeah, when I went to high school I was lucky to go out of the jurisdiction because at that point I was able to get into the music course in Newtown High, which because they had the only music academic school in the five boroughs in New York, I could get in and I didn’t have to go to one of those local high schools. And there I met Bobby Grosso, who is Joe Grosso’s son. And he was like I think maybe three or four years older than me. And it was through Bobby that I met his father Joe, who at that time was working at Lou Teresi’s Hickory Log, but had already made those wonderful Commodore records with Wild Bill and Muggsy and Pee Wee and all those people, and he was a regular guy there, he was with Bob Haggart or Miff Mole, and the people who matter — George Wettling, you know, guys who played the kind of music I liked at that time, Bobby Hackett played it better than — they all played it better than anybody else. And Joe — I used to eat at their house, and Joe would get up around noon, having worked the clubs ‘till four o’clock in the morning, and he would get up and come out in his long, silk bathrobe, holding a cigarette in a cigarette holder about that long you know, and I just thought that was the greatest life, to be able to finish work at four o’clock in the morning — be careful what you wish for. Well anyway, Joe used to take us down to the old Condon’s on West Third Street, you know, and you’d see all those guys that you heard on records and read about in the jazz magazines, in person. And so I was lucky. I had my own jazz band in school and Larry O’Brien was in it, the guy, I think he leads one of the Glenn Miller ghost bands. Yeah, he’s a very fine trombone player. He was my hot jazz trombone player, the guy who owned the Cork and Bib Club out in Queens was a high school buddy of mine also, Johnny Hearst played trumpet, and Bobby Grosso played the drums, and a few other people on bass and piano respectively.

Absolutely. Oh we were the only music guys in that high school, we all dressed with shirts, ties, suits and we all carried our own little jugs, you know, we were cool man. We didn’t know about smoking pot then, but we knew about drinking.
That came later. Not long later.
You had to graduate. You have to go through the different levels.
That’s it, right. The different sicknesses.
